content: The performance of laboratory services varies due to differing capacities among laboratories. This indicator does not evaluate the quality, cost, or effectiveness of the services provided. This is determined by the accuracy and reliability of diagnostic results, ensuring that laboratory quality keeps pace with the expansion of HIV testing services. The goal is to validate test results across the biomedical infrastructure, identify underperformance, and address weaknesses through enhanced supervision, equipment upgrades, and timely supply of reagents and equipment. This is a critical component of capacity-building for quality service delivery. The vacancy rate is assessed by the percentage of unfilled job positions, which helps evaluate whether planned health worker positions are adequately staffed and highlights recruitment and retention challenges.g., physicians, midwives, nurses) per 10,000 population. This indicator assesses whether there are sufficient healthcare workers to deliver services, with an accepted target of 23 professionals per 10,000 inhabitants. The number of annual new graduates from health workforce educational institutions is tracked to determine how many potential healthcare workers are being trained and prepared in the country. Peer educators, often recruited from civil society and connected to key populations, distribute condoms, sterile needles, and syringes (where permitted) and promote HIV testing. In some countries, they may also perform first-line HIV testing and refer individuals for further testing when needed. The availability of ART sites is assessed by the percentage of sites experiencing stock-outs of antiretroviral drugs (ARVs), diagnostic reagents, or co-trimoxazole (CTX). This indicator helps monitor stock management and supply chain efficiency. Rational ARV use is evaluated by the percentage of people living with HIV receiving ART in accordance with national guidelines. Consumption is assessed by the percentage of ARV quantities consumed during a reporting period, identifying potential overstock or stock-out risks. A ratio below 1 indicates cost efficiency, while a ratio above 1 suggests higher costs and the need for further investigation. ARV drug registration is assessed by the percentage of recommended ARV formulations registered in the country, which is essential for increasing access and affordability. Inventory control is evaluated by the percentage of ART sites submitting complete inventory reports on time, which is critical for effective procurement and supply management. If losses exceed 1%, further analysis and corrective action are required. Minimum stock levels are monitored by the percentage of ART sites placing orders when stock levels fall below the minimum threshold, highlighting risks of stock-outs. Strategic information systems are reviewed to assess data availability and identify gaps for improved planning. The percentage of indicator data published annually reflects the willingness of national authorities to share information with stakeholders. Completion of the National Commitments and Policies Instrument (NCPI) questionnaire for HIV/AIDS evaluates whether the country has a multisectoral strategic plan that includes all sectors and target populations, involves civil society, and aligns with national strategies. Health spending on HIV programs is assessed as a proportion of the national health budget, exploring options to increase contributions from public and international financing. Progress in domestic financing is tracked using a Relative Variation Index, with values greater than 1 indicating progress in self-sustained HIV responses. The unit cost of HIV interventions is tracked by per capita expenditure on HIV health programs, allowing for benchmarking against countries with similar income levels or epidemic burdens.
